messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The accident happened on a clear winter morning, two years ago, on the Beltway outside Richmond. Arthur, then still a state senator, was driving to a committee hearing when a pickup truck drifted across the median and struck his sedan head-on at highway speed. He remembers the impact not as a continuous event but as a series of frozen frames—the grille of the truck growing impossibly large, the windshield spiderwebbing, a single moment of pressure across his chest that he still feels as a sharp ache in his ribs whenever the memory surfaces. He was trapped in the wreckage for nearly forty minutes, and the smell of gasoline mixed with spilled bourbon from the other driver’s cab has never left him. When he tries to tell the story now, at his wife’s request or in a half-hearted attempt to explain his absences to colleagues, he finds himself losing the thread mid-sentence, unable to connect one picture to the next, and he trails off into silence.

Arthur is sixty-eight, a career politician who has spent thirty years in public life, and he had always prided himself on his composure. But in the months after the crash, he began to notice that the smell of alcohol at fundraisers or receptions—a volunteer’s wine glass, a lobbyist’s Scotch—would send a jolt through him, and he would find himself suddenly back in that frozen moment, the ache in his ribs flaring without warning. He had come to believe that the accident happened because of the sort of person he is: someone who was too careless, too distracted, too arrogant to see the danger coming. This conviction grew stronger each time a trigger caught him off guard. A car stopped oddly at an intersection, the sight of a damaged vehicle on the evening news, even the feel of his own sedan accelerating onto the highway—each one seemed to confirm that he was fundamentally exposed, that others could see what had happened to him just by looking at his face.

Because he was certain that danger could appear at any moment, Arthur began to wake during the night to check whether he was safe, lying still in the dark and listening for the wrong kind of silence. An unusual quiet in the house now felt to him like the moment before a disaster, and he would get up, walk through each room, verify that the doors were locked. This vigilance bled into his days. He had difficulty concentrating during meetings, his attention snagged by a car alarm outside or a sudden pause in conversation, and he found himself repeatedly blaming himself for the crash—dwelling on what he had done wrong, replaying his choices in the seconds before the impact, as if he could somehow punish himself into preparedness. The more he blamed himself, the more he felt that others could read the shame on him, and the more he scanned his surroundings for the next threat.

His driving became impossible. He avoided being behind the wheel entirely, and even as a passenger he felt the old pain in his ribs tighten with every turn. His wife drove him to appointments and events, but Arthur made excuses to cancel most of them. The rumination followed him everywhere. Each time he blamed himself, the memory returned with sharper physical force—the ache in his ribs, the smell of bourbon—and each time the memory surfaced, he blamed himself more. He started to believe that the only way to stay safe was to remain watchful, but the watchfulness itself brought back the frozen images, and the images brought back the shame, and the shame made him feel that he deserved whatever came next.

The cycle tightened over the course of a year. Arthur stopped attending committee hearings that required him to drive or to sit near anyone drinking. He told his staff he was working from home, but he spent most of his time in his study, staring at the wall, trying to hold the pictures of the crash at bay. His wife found him one night standing in the hallway at 3 a.m., listening to the silence. He could not explain what he was waiting for. What finally brought him to seek help was a single moment at a constituent dinner: a waiter uncorked a bottle of red wine near his table, and Arthur felt his ribs seize, his vision narrowing to a single frame of the truck’s grille, and he stood up and walked out without a word. His wife drove him home in silence. The next morning, she made an appointment with a therapist who specialized in trauma. Arthur is afraid of what he will find if he stops watching, but he is more afraid of what he has already lost—the career, the presence, the sense that he was ever in control.
